claim_verbatim: The AI data-centre build is not an overbuild. It will earn its cost because software, the largest buyer of AI output, was held back for decades by a shortage of people who could write code, and agents remove that shortage.
context: Opening paragraph (standfirst) of the essay, which continues: 'When the cost of code falls, the world buys more than proportionally more software. That demand, not the electricity going into the racks, decides whether the build pays.' X thread lead: 'The AI data-centre build is not an overbuild. Software was held back for decades by too few coders, and agents remove that limit.' (https://x.com/ctindale/status/2117972632645828703)
source: Substack essay 'Intelligence per watt: why the AI build earns its cost', ctindale.substack.com, 4 Nov 2026 13:01 UTC (5 Nov 2026 00:01 AEDT); X thread by @ctindale 4 Nov 2026 13:30 UTC (https://x.com/ctindale/status/2117972632645828703)
probability_words: is not an overbuild / will earn its cost (declarative; read as 'will')
mechanism: Agents remove the decades-long shortage of coders; cheaper code releases queued, supply-limited software demand (price elasticity about 1.4), so new software, not displaced wages, carries token revenue; revenue per GW is set by that demand, not by tokens per MW.
notes: Logged 5 Nov 2026. Headline thesis with no date or threshold of its own, so unscorable as worded and not queued in inferred-to-confirm.csv. He gives his own measurable test in the same essay: revenue per inference GW against the $10B rental and $20B breakeven (pl-114 to pl-117, stated) and his central figures (pl-120). Quoted as published.

claim_verbatim: My central call is the capped backlog model with elasticity varied: a 3.3% chance of falling below $10 billion in 2027 and 4.2% in 2029. Against the full $20 billion breakeven, the odds are 22% in 2027 and 18% in 2029, with a median 2029 revenue of $46 billion per inference GW.
context: Section 'How likely an overbuild is, by model' (Table 2: share of 2,400 runs per model in which revenue per inference GW falls below the $10B rental). He names the capped backlog model as his central call; the two-tier model without the software backlog gives 47% (2027) and 41% (2029), which he rejects because it 'describe[s] a world in which cheaper code creates no new software. The thesis says that world does not exist.' X thread: 'The odds: revenue per inference GW falls below the $10B rental in 3.3% of runs in 2027 and 4.2% in 2029; below the $20B breakeven in 22% and 18%.' (https://x.com/ctindale/status/2117972633618882805)

claim_verbatim: The thesis requires the world’s software spending to more than double by 2029. ... That doubling is plausible for the reason the thesis gives.
context: Section 'The size of the pool, and what the thesis requires'. Gartner puts 2026 spending at $1.468 trillion on software and $1.570 trillion on IT services ($3.04 trillion together). His capped model's 2029 new-software token line is $1.69 trillion; with tokens at half the cost of agent-built software, 'about $3.4 trillion of new software work a year, on top of today's spending.'

claim_verbatim: The demand is there. The risk sits in how the capacity was financed: a lender that has lent short against assets with a long payback needs revenue every quarter. The data centres will not stand empty.
context: Section 'Revenue arrives after the build'. He names GPU rental companies financed with expensive debt as the firms exposed: CoreWeave had $51.6 billion of total debt in Oct 2026 (from $29.8 billion at end 2025), Q2 interest expense $640 million against an operating loss of $49 million, a $104 billion revenue backlog at 30 Jun 2026, and new Q3 contracts at about $40 million annualised revenue per MW.
source: Substack essay 'Intelligence per watt: why the AI build earns its cost', ctindale.substack.com, 4 Nov 2026 13:01 UTC (5 Nov 2026 00:01 AEDT); X thread by @ctindale 4 Nov 2026 13:30 UTC (https://x.com/ctindale/status/2117972632645828703)
mechanism: Software demand fills the capacity; any failure comes from short-dated debt financing at GPU renters (neoclouds such as CoreWeave), not from empty data centres.
notes: Logged 5 Nov 2026. No date or utilisation threshold, so unscorable and not queued. Two linked readings for later review: AI data-centre utilisation stays high, and stress, if it comes, shows first in neocloud debt rather than idle capacity. Quoted as published.

claim_verbatim: What would prove this wrong Mid-level and senior developer wages falling more than 20% for each one-third rise in effective coding supply. That puts the labour elasticity below about 1.3, under the central case. A 25% fall puts it at 1.0. METR’s doubling time stretching to nine months or longer. Spending on AI-built software below $300 billion in 2027. The central path needs about $500 billion of new-software tokens. Data-centre lease renewals in 2026 below $10 billion per GW.
context: Section 'What would prove this wrong' (his own self-critique for this major position). X thread: 'What would prove me wrong: mid and senior developer wages down >20% per one-third rise in coding supply, METR's doubling time stretching to 9 months, AI-built software spend under $300B in 2027, or 2026 lease renewals under $10B per GW.' (https://x.com/ctindale/status/2117972633946103874). He also lists 'The evidence against' (Stanford/ADP: developers aged 22 to 25 about 20% below late-2022 peak; Federal Reserve paper: US coder employment about 500,000 below pre-ChatGPT trend) and says 'Neither changes the verdict.'
